review.summary: The prior MAJOR is substantially fixed. Exact-tuple dedupe happens before the budget, the 100-viewer one-hour case is supported, and a limit hit preserves the independent metrics. One availability residual remains. The 1,000,000-row aggregate budget is far above any measured cost, because the heavy-scale cost was only measured per person at 10k rows. The committed receipt also does not match the numbers quoted in this review, and the aggregate cap branch has no unit test. No correctness regression found in the arithmetic, scope checks or dedupe. Verdict: no BLOCKER; one MAJOR (unmeasured worst-case aggregate CPU), two MINOR.

findings.issue: The aggregate budget of 1,000,000 unique rows bounds row count, not CPU. The worst-case cost at that budget was never measured and extrapolates to tens of seconds of synchronous BigInt work.
findings.evidence: The receipt shows near-cap LCM histories cost about 0.5-0.9 s per person at 10k rows (epoch_week_spread, scale_durations). Per-person cap 10,000 × aggregate cap 1,000,000 permits 100 such persons in one call, roughly 50-90 s on the event loop. The only cohort benchmark (72,000 rows, 246 ms) uses uniform 5000 ms segments, so the scale stays at 5000 and it is the cheapest case. The 100×10k heavy-scale cohort is neither benchmarked nor tested.
findings.impact: Within the stated supported envelope, a report on a large cohort with jittered, non-uniform sample durations can block the Node event loop for a minute or more. That is the same availability class as the prior MAJOR, just at a higher threshold.
findings.recommended_fix: Either (a) add a CPU-proportional work budget, for example sum over persons of rows × scaleBits (or rows × log2 iterations), and return limit_exceeded when it is exceeded, or (b) measure the worst-case 100×10,000 heavy-scale cohort and lower MAX_REPORT_COMPLETION_SEGMENTS or keep the function off request paths. Document the measured ceiling next to the constant. Keep the explicit requirement that the adapter run large histories in background or materialized jobs.
findings.required_test: A benchmark and receipt for 100 persons × 10,000 unique rows with durations spread across 1..5000 (and epoch-scale timestamps), asserting a recorded wall-clock budget. Also a unit test that the work budget returns limit_exceeded before any BigInt work.

findings.issue: The committed receipt does not match the benchmark figures quoted for this review, and it omits several claimed checks.
findings.evidence: Quoted: 72000 rows 280 ms; epoch spread median 541/615 ms, max 611/661 ms. The receipt records 72000 rows at 246 ms, epoch_week_spread_5000 median 825 / max 900, and epoch_week_spread_5600 median 720 / max 880. The receipt has no entry for the mixed 7/11/13 oracle, the 1..5000 / 1..5800 cap pins, or the double-6000 duplicate case. The 72k check's `equal` only inspects completionRate and averageViewingSeconds, not attendance or order results.
findings.impact: The reviewed claims are not reproducible from the checked-in artifact. A reader cannot tell which run the stated numbers came from, or whether the receipt is stale.
findings.recommended_fix: Regenerate and commit the receipt from the final source with the performance-check.mjs run (record git SHA and source hash), or correct the quoted numbers. Extend the 72k check to compare the full CoreMetrics output with expected values.
findings.required_test: Re-run performance-check.mjs on the final tree. Assert that the receipt's status is PASS, its sources match, and it includes the 72k cohort with full-output equality.

findings.issue: The new aggregate budget branch (MAX_REPORT_COMPLETION_SEGMENTS) has no unit test. The only limit test exercises the per-person 10,000 cap.
findings.evidence: The 10001-row test uses one person (person-0), so it hits the firstCompletionTime limit and never the aggregate `> MAX_REPORT_COMPLETION_SEGMENTS` check. Nothing pins exactly 1,000,000 available versus 1,000,001 unavailable, or that the aggregate limit applies across persons when each person is under 10k.
findings.impact: A regression that changes the constant, or breaks the count-after-dedupe logic, would go undetected. That is the exact fix being closed here.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a cheap test: 101 persons × 10,000 unique rows exceeds the aggregate cap and fails fast, with attendance and average viewing preserved and completion/order returning limit_exceeded. Optionally add a boundary test at exactly the cap with a trivially cheap uniform scale.
findings.required_test: Unit test asserting completionRate and postCompletionOrderRate are {unavailable, limit_exceeded} for 101×10,000 unique rows, while attendanceRate and averageViewingSeconds stay available and correct.
